OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Specify the epidemiology, etiology, and risk factors of Freiberg infraction.
Perform an appropriate workup of patients in whom Freiberg infraction is suspected.
Specify the surgical and nonsurgical management of Freiberg infraction.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Freiberg infraction, also known as Freiberg disease, and its management was initially reported
on in 1914.1
The term infraction is a combination of the terms infarction and fracture2 (Resource 1).




NOTES

Freiberg infraction initially involves the dorsal aspect of a lesser metatarsal head, and in
advanced stages may involve the remainder of the metatarsal head and the proximal
phalangeal base.

Epidemiology
Freiberg infraction most commonly involves the second metatarsal head (68% of
patients), followed by the third metatarsal head (27%), fourth metatarsal head (3%),
and fifth metatarsal head (<2%).3
Freiberg infraction is approximately 5 times more common in females than males and
presents unilaterally more than 90% of the time.3,4
Freiberg infraction is most commonly seen during the second and third decades of life
but may present later.4
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The anatomy of a lesser toe metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint is partially demonstrated in
Figure 1.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Freiberg Infraction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000013
2/27

Figure 1 Lateral view illustration of the metatarsal and phalanges of a representative lesser toe.
The lumbrical and interosseous muscles pass plantar to the axis of motion of the
metatarsophalangeal joint and act as flexors of that joint. They pass dorsal to the interphalangeal
joints and act as extensors of those joints. (Reproduced from Mizel MS, Yodlowski ML: Disorders
of the lesser metatarsophalangeal joints. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 1995;3[3]:166-173.)

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Typically, there is a fat pad resting underneath the lesser metatarsal head that has
attachments to the proximal phalangeal base. MTP joint dorsiflexion during normal gait
leads to distal migration of this fat pad, which increases biomechanical stress on the
metatarsal head.
Soft-tissue and/or bone impingement and soft-tissue contracture may lead to decreased
MTP range of motion, particularly dorsiflexion.
Etiology
The exact etiology of Freiberg infraction is unknown. Proposed etiologies include
osteonecrosis secondary to acute or repetitive vascular injury, arterial insufficiency, repetitive
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Freiberg Infraction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000013
3/27

trauma/stress leading to microfractures, dorsal mechanical impingement, and genetic
predisposition.3
Natural History
Patients with Freiberg infraction may be asymptomatic or become asymptomatic over time or
with nonsurgical treatment. Alternatively, it may progress with metatarsal head collapse or
end-stage arthritis of the MTP joint.
Risk Factors
Previous trauma, diabetes mellitus, systemic lupus erythematosus, and hypercoagulability
have been linked to Freiberg infraction.4
Classification
The most common classification system for Freiberg infraction was developed by Smillie and is
shown in Figure 2 and Table 1 (Resource 2).3,5
Alternative classification systems have been described by Gauthier and Elbaz and Thompson
and Hamilton.3,6,7
Table 1 Smillie Classification of Metatarsal Head Degeneration
Stage
Description
I
Fissure in epiphysis with sclerosis between cancellous surfaces is present.
II
Absorption of cancellous bone occurs on the proximal side with sinking of the
articular cartilage dorsally.
III
Further absorption and sinking of the articular surface occur with bony projections
medially and laterally. Exostosis is present on the dorsal proximal metatarsal head.
IV
The articular surface has sunk so far that the opportunity for restoration of normal
anatomy has passed. Fractures of the medial and lateral projections may occur.
V
Arthrosis with flattening and deformity of the metatarsal head is present. The
plantar aspect is the only area where cartilage retains its original contour. The

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Patients may complain of pain, swelling, and stiffness of the affected MTP joint that is
exacerbated by activity, walking barefoot, or flexible or high-heel shoes.
Physical Examination
In the early stages of the disease, tenderness, swelling, and decreased range of motion of the
affected MTP joint may be present.
Plantar callosities under the metatarsal head or an associated hammer or claw toe deformity
may be present.
Contracture of the triceps surae may be present, with involvement of the gastrocnemius more
common than the soleus.
In later stages of the disease, palpable osteophytes of the metatarsal head and phalangeal
base may be present.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Initial radiographs may be normal in patients with Smillie stage I Freiberg infraction, which is
not associated with articular collapse.
In patients with more advanced stages, radiographic findings may demonstrate dorsal collapse
of the metatarsal head, flattening of the metatarsal head with subchondral sclerosis and
metatarsal head exostoses, intra-articular fractures and loose bodies, and progressive joint-
space narrowing or obliteration with proximal phalangeal base exostoses (Figure 3, A).
Computed Tomography
CT is less commonly performed than MRI but may show the extent and location of exostoses,
fractures, loose bodies, and subchondral collapse (Figure 3, B).
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Freiberg Infraction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000013
6/27

MRI may show patchy edema and evidence of osteonecrosis in the metatarsal head in patients
with Smillie stage I Freiberg infraction before radiographic changes are evident. MRI may be
helpful in surgical planning with respect to the extent of metatarsal head and proximal
phalangeal base involvement and in assessing for the presence and degree of concurrent foot
pathology (Figure 3, C).
Figure 3 Images of the foot of a 52-year-old woman with Smillie stage 4 Freiberg infraction. A,
Oblique foot radiograph demonstrates depression of the second metatarsal head. B, Sagittal CT
scan shows collapse of a portion of the dorsal and central metatarsal head and a dorsal loose
body. C, Sagittal T2-weighted MRI shows edema in the metatarsal head greater than the proximal
phalangeal base and dorsal depression. (Image courtesy of Michael S. Aronow, MD, Farmington
CT.)
Bone Scintigraphy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Freiberg Infraction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000013
7/27

Although not routinely performed, bone scans may show photopenic defect in the affected
metatarsal head in patients in the early avascular stages and increased activity localized to the
affected metatarsal head in patients in the more advanced stages (Figure 4; Resource 3).
Figure 4 Bone scan of bilateral feet shows increased radionuclide uptake in the third metatarsal
head of the right foot of a patient with symptomatic Freiberg infraction. (Reproduced from
Shereff MJ: Freiberg’s infraction, in Nunley JA, Pfeffer GB, Sanders RW, Trepman E, eds: Advanced
Reconstruction: Foot and Ankle. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2004,
pp 253-258.)
Diagnosis
The diagnosis is made based on the patient history, physical examination findings, and
imaging study findings.
Differential Diagnosis
The differential diagnosis includes metatarsalgia; MTP instability; posttraumatic arthritis;
inflammatory arthritis; MTP synovitis secondary to biomechanical stress from a long or
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Freiberg Infraction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000013
8/27

plantar-flexed second metatarsal or first ray hypermobility; acute fracture; stress fracture;
interdigital neuritis/Morton neuroma; and other causes of osteonecrosis, such as previous oral
corticosteroid use ( Videos 1 and 2).
Video 1 Interdigital (Morton) neuroma test, in Armstrong AD, Hubbard MC, eds: Essentials of
Musculoskeletal Care, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016.
SEND FEEDBACK

Video 2 Interdigital (Morton) neuroma injection, in Armstrong AD, Hubbard MC, eds: Essentials of
Musculoskeletal Care, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Initial management includes offloading the affected metatarsal head and resting the affected
MTP joint. A low-heel shoe with a stiff forefoot rocker, a turf toe plate or a rigid carbon fiber
orthosis under a cushioned insole, and/or taping of the affected toe may be used to limit MTP
dorsiflexion during gait, resting the joint and maintaining the fat pad under the metatarsal
head. An insole with a depression under the affected metatarsal head or metatarsal pad
proximal to it may be considered. For more refractory cases, a period of immobilization in a
controlled ankle motion walker or a weight-bearing short leg walking cast with a toe plate may
be used.
Calf stretching with the hindfoot in neutral supination and the knee in extension may offload
the forefoot.
Oral or topical analgesic agents, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medication or
acetaminophen, may be beneficial.
An intra-articular corticosteroid injection may afford pain relief for synovitis not responsive to
the above measures or in patients with end-stage arthritis. After injection, strong
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Freiberg Infraction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000013
10/27

consideration should be made for protecting the MTP joint via taping to decrease the risk of
capsule/ligamentous attenuation, leading to an iatrogenic transverse or sagittal plane
deformity.

Nonsurgical Management
Orthobiologic injections, such as platelet-rich plasma, stem cells, and amniotic tissue,
may have a future role with respect to joint inflammation and cartilage integrity but do
not address the biomechanical pathology, are expensive, and have minimal support in
the literature to date for the management of Freiberg infraction.
Surgical Management
Isolated synovectomy, open or arthroscopic débridement, and exostectomy of the joint may
be effective, particularly in patients with less advanced stages.8,9 Microfracture or retrograde
drilling of osteochondral lesions may be performed. Core decompression also has been
described.10
A dorsal closing wedge osteotomy of the metatarsal head may be used to rotate the more
normal plantar metatarsal head dorsally so that it is articulating with proximal phalangeal base
cartilage during gait rather than the damaged central cartilage.
The metatarsal osteotomy may be intra-articular,6,11-17 in which the diseased cartilage is
excised as part of the closing-wedge osteotomy, or extra-articular.18-22 An arthroscopic
technique for performing an intra-articular closing-wedge osteotomy has been described14
(Video 3).
Osteotomies generally are not necessary for patients with Smillie stage I Freiberg infraction
and generally are less effective as the amount of cartilage involvement increases; however, the
addition of external distraction may be beneficial if performed in patients with Smillie stage IV
or state V Freiberg infraction.17 Smillie performed elevation of depressed articular fragments
with the use of cancellous bone graft.5
For large osteochondral defects, an osteochondral autograft from the lateral femoral
condyle,11,12,23,24 lateral talus,11 or dorsal first metatarsal head or an osteochondral
allograft25 may be considered.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Freiberg Infraction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000013
11/27

Partial head resection (DuVries arthroplasty) may be considered in patients with end-stage
arthritis or in whom a previous joint-sparing procedure failed. Complete metatarsal head
resection is an alternative but is not recommended by some studies because of the risk of
transfer metatarsalgia. Consideration may be given to adding interposition of local capsular
and periosteal tissue;26 autograft tendon, such as the extensor digitorum brevis27,28 or a
portion of the extensor hallucis longus;29 or allograft, including umbilical tissue.
Implant arthroplasty is associated with mixed results. Historically, silastic implants have been
used with some good results but are associated with high complication rates, including
implant breakdown and adjacent bone destruction.3,30 More recently, a polyvinyl alcohol
hydrogel implant has been used.31-33
Video 3 Guyton GP: Proximal crescentic metatarsal osteotomy, in Campbell JT, ed: Surgical
Techniques in Orthopaedics: Hallux Valgus. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2006.

Surgical Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Freiberg Infraction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000013
12/27

The associated shortening of the metatarsal and elevation of the metatarsal head also
decreases the biomechanical stress on the remaining articular cartilage. If additional
shortening is required, the plantar aspect of the osteotomy may be completed and
additional bone removed and/or the distal fragment translated proximally.
Isolated case reports have been published on patients treated with subchondroplasty via
percutaneously injected calcium phosphate34 and micronized allograft cartilage
matrix.35
Although lesser MTP fusion and amputation are possible primary treatment options, the
author of this lesson is unaware of any reports in the literature with respect to Freiberg
infraction and would not recommend such treatment options at this time.
Indications
Surgical treatment is indicated for symptomatic patients not responsive to appropriate
nonsurgical treatment. Given the relatively young age of many patients with Frieberg infraction
and the reported results of the alternative procedures available, caution may be advised with
respect to implant arthroplasty.
Contraindications
Potential contraindications include likely noncompliance with postoperative management,
substantial medical comorbidities, poor vascular status, and active infection.
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
The extent of disease that needs to be addressed is determined via preoperative planning. Any
concurrent pathology , such as an associated hammer toe deformity or extensor tendon
contracture, may need to be addressed.
Positioning
The patient is placed in the supine position. The use of a tourniquet is optional.SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Freiberg Infraction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000013
13/27

Surgical Approaches
A dorsal approach centered over the affected metatarsal head or adjacent intermetatarsal
space typically is used.
The joint is initially débrided, and exostoses are removed.
A technique for intra-articular dorsal closing wedge metatarsal osteotomy is shown in Figures
5 and 6.16

A technique for tissue interposition arthroplasty is shown in Figure 10.26
Figure 10 Intraoperative photographs of a foot show the technique for tissue interposition
arthroplasty. A, The extensor hood is incised, and the extensor mechanism is retracted. B, A flap
of periosteum and fat is elevated from the dorsum of the metatarsal; this may expose part of the
interossei on either side. This must remain attached to the base of the proximal phalanx and care
must be taken at the joint level because the capsule is the weakest part of the flap. C, The joint is
exposed; it is preferable to retain the collateral ligaments. D, Débridement is performed to round
it off and shorten the metatarsal head. The dorsal head can be reduced; the plantar cartilage
does not require débridement. The dorsum of the proximal phalanx also can be débrided. Ensure
that full range of motion is possible. E, The end of the flap is grasped loosely distally with the use
of forceps and then rolled into a rollmop. F, This is sutured through the limbs of the forceps to
create the rollmop graft. One limb of the suture should be long. G, The longer limb is sutured
through the plantar plate to stabilize the graft in the joint. H, The long limb is pulled, drawing the
graft as far into the joint as required to create a cushion on the central and dorsal aspects of the
joint, and then tied off. (Reproduced with permission from Abdul W, Hickey B, Perera A:
Functional outcomes of local pedicle graft interpositional arthroplasty in adults with severe
Freiberg's disease. Foot Ankle Int 2018;39[11]:1290-1300.)
Postoperative Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Freiberg Infraction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000013
19/27

After metatarsal osteotomy, the patient typically is instructed to remain forefoot non–weight
bearing in a short leg cast with a toe plate or a heel–weight-bearing shoe for at least 4 to 6
weeks postoperatively until sufficient radiographic and clinical bone healing has occurred.
After isolated débridement, interposition arthroplasty, implant arthroplasty, and in some
metatarsal osteotomy procedures that result in stable fixation and good bone quality, weight
bearing may be initiated earlier with the use of a rigid soled shoe. Sutures are removed 2 to 3
weeks postoperatively after wound healing has occurred, at which point gentle passive and
active MTP range-of-motion exercises are initiated.
Complications
Potential complications include nonresolution of symptoms, progressive arthritis, osteotomy
malunion/nonunion, floating toe, MTP joint stiffness, weakness, symptomatic hardware,
transfer metatarsalgia, infection, wound dehiscence, vascular compromise, nerve injury, and
complex regional pain syndrome.
Outcomes
Smillie stage 1 Freiberg infraction often responds to nonsurgical management.
The results of metatarsal osteotomy are partially summarized in Table 2.
Osteochondral autograft had at least equivalent improvement compared with intra-articular
metatarsal osteotomy in patients with Smillie stage III, stage IV, or stage V Freiberg infraction in
a prospective randomized controlled study,11 and substantially better outcomes with less
complications in a retrospective comparative study.12
Interposition arthroplasty with the use of a local periosteal tissue was performed in 25 feet of
23 patients. Five feet were Smillie stage III Freiberg infraction, 12 feet were Smillie stage IV
Freiberg infraction, and 8 feet were stage V Freiberg infraction. Substantial improvement was
reported in visual analog scale pain scores, American Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society scores,
and Manchester-Oxford Foot Questionnaire scores, as well as ability to wear shoes and return
to athletics. One superficial wound infection was reported, one patient did not note
improvement, and no transfer metatarsalgia occurred.26

Outcomes
Polyvinyl alcohol hydrogel implant is associated with mixed short-term results. One
study reported overall clinical improvement in Patient-Reported Outcome Measurement
Information System scores in 14 second or third MTP joints in 13 patients, four of whom
had Freiberg infraction; however, five complications, including one revision procedure
with implant removal and bone graft and one fractured implant likely requiring future
revision, ocurred.32 In another study retrospectively comparing six patients who had
polyvinyl alcohol hydrogel implants and seven patients who had intra-articular
metatarsal osteotomies, of which three and two patients had Frieberg’s infraction,
respectively, four of the polyvinyl alcohol hydrogel implants were revised to metatarsal
osteotomies within 15 months, whereas none of metatarsal osteotomies were revised.31
